overview: This atlas record is best read as British colonial Ceylon after the 1815 takeover of the Kandyan kingdom, not as the birth of an island or a single civilization. A British Crown colony already existed on the coasts from 1802; islandwide British control followed in 1815. The eight imported polygons trace one coarse island outline through 1945. That endpoint is an atlas shortcut: colonial rule legally ended on 4 February 1948. Within this state lived many communities whose languages, religions, family systems, livelihoods and political aims differed. Roads, railways, schools, medicine, plantations and archives expanded unevenly, often through coercion and unequal labour; resistance and organizing accompanied them. The people and their histories continued beyond both atlas dates.

periods.title: Convention, occupation and Uva-Wellassa resistance
periods.summary: British officials and Kandyan chiefs signed the 1815 Convention, but rule was contested almost immediately. Resistance spread from 1817; capture of leaders, possession of the Tooth Relic and ruthless suppression helped the colonial state consolidate power.

periods.title: Rule through Kandyan commissioners
periods.summary: After the rebellion, colonial officials governed the interior through a separate Board of Kandyan Commissioners. This was a period of consolidation and documentation, not quiet consent; the surviving board records begin in 1815 and run to the 1833 administrative reorganization.

periods.title: Colebrooke-Cameron reorganization
periods.summary: Executive and Legislative Councils, five provinces and an islandwide judicial structure tied the colony together administratively. Rajakariya compulsory labour was formally abolished, while authority still rested with a colonial governor and limited appointed representation.

periods.title: Tax resistance, coffee expansion and the first railway
periods.summary: The 1848 protest opposed road labour and new taxes amid land loss, and ended under martial law. Coffee plantations, roads and then railways transformed parts of the highlands for export; the first rail service began in 1864.

periods.title: Coffee rust, tea plantations and migrant labour
periods.summary: Coffee rust appeared in 1869 and coffee collapsed over the next decade. Tea estates expanded with year-round labour, drawing large numbers of workers from South India through systems that were essential to the export economy but weakly regulated for much of the century.

periods.title: Limited election and the repression of 1915
periods.summary: The 1910 reforms introduced only four elected non-official Legislative Council seats. During the 1915 riots, martial law and court-martial punishment exposed the violence of colonial emergency power and helped sharpen demands for political change.

periods.title: Congress, unions and demands for the vote
periods.summary: The Ceylon National Congress sought a common reform movement but fractured over representation. Labour organizers formed a union in 1922, led a 1923 general strike and pressed for adult suffrage across gender, caste, religion and ethnicity.

periods.title: Universal suffrage, State Council and malaria crisis
periods.summary: The Donoughmore system brought universal adult suffrage and a State Council in 1931, after women had organized and testified for the vote. The political opening coexisted with grave inequality and the 1934-1935 malaria epidemic, which sickened about 1.5 million people.

periods.title: Wartime colony and the atlas cutoff
periods.summary: Ceylon remained a British colony through the Second World War. The Soulbury Commission introduced a Westminster model in 1944, but the atlas changes the island label in 1945 before the 1947 Independence Act and independence in 1948.

sections.title: How to read this map record

items.text: The atlas record is a state-shaped label, not the name of one ancient people. Coverage marks Ceylon from 1815 to 1945 with approximate dates and eight consecutive polygons. This card therefore follows British colonial administration after the Kandyan takeover without treating a government name as one culture or a complete biography of the island's people.

The 1800 atlas geometry makes the transition unusually visible. Its feature called ceylon-dutch-1800 is the island outline with a hole; that hole is exactly the separate Kandy polygon. In 1815 the hole disappears and the new ceylon-1815 record uses the same outer ring. This encodes a coastal-plus-interior merger, not proof that every community accepted the Convention.

Each colonial snapshot is a single 35-position island polygon. Across all eight intervals there are only three exact coordinate variants, with about 0.001 degrees of edge jitter from first to last. Those tiny shifts are basemap redrawing, not changing coastlines, battle fronts or administrative borders.

At 1815 the mainland British East India Company polygon has a bounding box that reaches the island's latitude; later British Raj and a 1938 United Kingdom occurrence do too. Polygon intersection tests are false in every snapshot. Mysore and Travancore are nearby mainland records, not overlapping Ceylon. A bounding box is a filing cabinet, not a border.

The 1945 Sri Lanka polygon has the same 35-point broad outline but is not coordinate-identical to the 1938-1945 Ceylon ring. More important, the label change is three years early: the colony did not become independent until 4 February 1948. Map handoffs are navigation aids, not constitutional documents.

The March 1815 Convention transferred the Kandyan kingdom's sovereignty to Britain in Article 4 and promised protection of Buddhism and its customs in Article 5. It was an agreement among British authorities and Kandyan chiefs amid political manoeuvring. It must not be retold as a vote by the island's whole population.

John D'Oyly shows how scholarship could become an instrument of conquest. He learned Sinhala language and literature from respected teachers and built relationships with monks, poets and nobles; British authorities also employed him as a spy to split the Kandyan court. Knowing a language is not the same as respecting its speakers' political freedom.

Resistance spread through the Kandyan regions in 1817-1818. British forces captured leaders and recovered the Tooth Relic, whose custody was treated as political legitimacy; the archive also calls the suppression ruthless. A colonial proclamation branded nineteen chiefs traitors, a designation formally invalidated in 2016.

The 1833 reforms created Executive and Legislative Councils, divided the island into five provinces and proposed one judicial structure. They also abolished rajakariya compulsory labour. These were large administrative changes, but the appointed colonial councils did not amount to self-government or equal political power.

In 1848 Dumbara residents said a road ordinance had brought compulsory labour back. Around 3,000 unarmed people gathered at the Kandy Kachcheri to petition against road, shop, gun and dog taxes; ancestral land loss under an 1840 Crown Lands ordinance may also have mattered. Violence followed, and the British imposed martial law.

The 1915 crisis involved riots as well as severe colonial repression. Martial law authorized shooting alleged rioters without trial or showing cause; Edward Henry Pedris was court-martialled and executed, and Sinhala leaders were jailed. The National Archives page foregrounds that repression, so it should not be treated as a complete account of violence suffered by Muslim communities during the riots.

Coffee expansion was an imperial project as well as a crop story. Governors supported planters, sold central-hill land cheaply, financed experiments and roads, and cleared forest for estates. Coffee rust appeared in 1869 and destroyed the industry over roughly a decade. Colonial profits and infrastructure came with environmental transformation and little local political control.

James Taylor was processing tea leaves on a bungalow veranda by 1866, planted twenty acres and sent an early shipment of just 23 pounds. That is small enough to imagine lifting, although nobody should try carrying a tea industry in a school backpack. The Tea Board credits the first successful Ceylon planter while acknowledging earlier attempts.

Tea and coffee relied heavily on migrant workers from South India. A peer-reviewed study describes export monocultures dependent on imported wage labour and a kangany system that recruited and coordinated workers while colonial regulation remained weak. Families who made lives on estates were people and communities, not simply a labour supply.

Rail began in 1864 chiefly to move coffee from Kandy's highlands to Colombo; tea then drove further construction. Trains also carried workers, machinery, fertilizer, rice and other food, and later more passengers. The engineering connected places, but its first routes followed the export economy's priorities rather than an equal islandwide travel plan.

A Central Bank retrospective separates the plantation export economy from rural subsistence farming. More than 90 percent of exports were plantation products, while rural communities received negligible benefit from plantation growth and the colony imported many consumer goods, including food. A booming export graph could therefore coexist with a struggling household budget.

Colonial governments renovated many irrigation works, and that mattered to farming. Yet the island's reservoir and canal traditions were already more than two millennia old. Calling every repaired tank a British invention would be like fixing an old bicycle and claiming you invented wheels; renovation and origin are different achievements.

sections.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life

items.text: A museum in Gampola uses line rooms more than a century old to reconstruct estate-worker life. One roughly 100-square-foot room represents a whole home, with clay walls, hanging pots and pans, and a basic hearth. It conveys crowding and domestic work on plantations, but it is a modern reconstruction and cannot stand for every worker, estate or decade.

Under older Kandyan law, household location could shape inheritance. A later court explained binna marriage as the husband joining the wife's parental home so she retained parental-property rights; in diga she moved to his home and usually lost them, with exceptions. This is a Kandyan legal pattern, not a rule for Tamil, Muslim, low-country or every Kandyan family.

Meals differed by ecology, income, religion and community. A later FAO study describes a dry-zone pattern of rice on irrigated land mainly for home use and other foods on dry land for home and market. Combined with the colonial plantation-versus-subsistence split, it suggests why an export crop tells us little about what any particular child ate for dinner.

A shore-seine boat model preserves clever coastal engineering: full-size planks were literally sewn together with coconut-fibre rope, with leaves used to waterproof the seams. Variants worked along western, southern and northeastern coasts. Boats could need stitches without being sick, but the museum label cannot tell us the lives of every fisher who used one.

A nineteenth-century painted wood mask from the island's interior has coiled-cobra forms dramatic enough to win a staring contest. Its 1886 purchase from a dealer leaves major gaps: the catalog does not name its maker, exact community or performance. The object documents skilled carving and colonial collecting, not one islandwide belief.

Clothing cannot responsibly be reduced to a single Ceylon costume. Museum catalogues include Buddhist robes and cloths acquired in Sri Lanka, but often provide little production date, maker or wearing context. Dress varied with community, religion, occupation, gender, wealth, weather and occasion; a monk's robe is evidence of a robe, not everyone's wardrobe.

A nineteenth-century betel-nut cutter associated with Kandy also records a collecting relationship. The British Museum says colonial official Hugh Nevill assembled objects with sparse provenance and likely obtained this cutter through the Kandyan Society of Arts. The little tool shows craft and social practice, while its museum journey warns how much maker information empire could discard.

sections.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence

items.text: Learning did not begin with colonial schools. A UNESCO-hosted history describes oral teaching and memorization around Buddhist temples, later ola-leaf manuscripts and libraries, and pirivena colleges for clergy and some male lay students. It also shows a limit: these institutions did not provide the same access to every child, gender or religious community.

British rule expanded schooling through an unequal dual structure. Church-assisted English schools attracted elites, while state vernacular schools served common people; pirivenas continued beside them. A Department of Public Instruction began in 1869. More schools mattered, but language, class, gender, religion and place still shaped who could attend and what schooling promised.

A period Tamil sample is உதய தாரகை, transliterated utayatārakai and translated “Morning Star.” It is the title on a bilingual Tamil-English issue printed in the Jaffna mission world on 15 April 1841. Tamil is a Brahmi-derived abugida. This is a verified newspaper title, not a spoken sentence, not Sinhala, and not proof that every Tamil person read mission print.

Writing also appeared on objects, but not every inscription can be translated from a catalog. A hinged brass box acquired in Kandy in 1895 is labelled as carrying Tamil writing; the museum gives neither its production date nor the inscription text. It is evidence of an inscribed object and of missing documentation, so this card does not invent a reading.

Archives make colonial government visible, but their silences matter. Holdings include Kandyan commissioners, Kachcheri offices, inquiries, newspapers, maps, the 1818 rebellion and political organizations. These files are powerful evidence about administration and petitions; they preserve far less of conversations at a hearth, a child's game or a worker's unrecorded complaint.

Government archaeology took shape through surveys, photographs and inscription work from the 1860s, with an official department from 1890. Work at Anuradhapura, Sigiriya and Polonnaruwa documented buildings, inscriptions and murals, including mural finds reported in 1897. The department organized research; it did not create the ancient sites or the knowledge local communities held about them.

The Archaeology Department now hosts scholarship criticizing its own colonial inheritance. One conference paper says early institutions privileged Western ideas and excluded local voices, and urges comparison with local texts and traditions. So “discovery” in this card means something entered an official survey or archive, not that Sri Lankans had forgotten their own heritage.

People used more than one medical system. Sri Lanka's Department of Ayurveda names Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Deshiya Chikitsa as distinct living traditions. Its 2024 policy is modern evidence for plurality and continuity, not a time machine telling us exactly which remedy every nineteenth-century family used.

Early British medical services mainly served the military and kept civil institutions under military control. A separate Civil Medical Department in 1858 marked a civilian administrative phase. That institutional milestone did not erase local healers, guarantee equal rural access or make colonial health policy purely benevolent.

Colonial institutions trained more health workers over time: Colombo Medical College opened in 1870, a local nursing school in 1878, and women entered the medical college in 1892. Civil birth and death registration began in 1867 and a bacteriology laboratory in 1900. These were durable institutions, though the timeline alone does not prove equal service.

Colombo planned sewers from 1896, started construction in 1906 and completed much of the system by 1925. This was city infrastructure, not an islandwide flush-toilet switch. The municipal page says even a 1972 plan found many residents using on-site systems and some with no facility, which makes broad claims about colonial household plumbing especially unsafe.

A 1917 Colombo health report urged connecting latrines to sewers and controlling flies, refuse and manure near homes to reduce enteric fever, dysentery and infant diarrhoea. It shows officials linking toilets, waste, water and disease. It also speaks in a colonial inspector's voice, so residents' constraints and knowledge are mostly absent.

School toilets and water were still inadequate in 1928. Colonial inspectors counted 3,106 schools serving 554,595 children, but only 2,649 schools with latrines, 493 with urinals and 991 with protected wells. Even those totals do not prove every fixture worked or every child could use it safely; a toilet count is not the same as a good toilet.

The 1934-1935 malaria epidemic affected about 1.5 million people and killed nearly 80,000. Responses used quinine, mobile medical units, drainage and other environmental work, oiling and larvicides such as Paris green; DDT came later. The scale makes this a history of loss and organized public health, not a cheerful tale of one miracle chemical.

Help also came through political and community organizing. The Suriya-Mal movement brought medicine, food and supplies to distant communities during the malaria crisis and supported education for children treated as lower caste. Its 1933 founding and welfare work show young activists linking anti-imperial politics to daily survival.

sections.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule

items.text: The “elective principle” of 1910 was a narrow opening. Of ten non-official Legislative Council members, only four were elected, and those seats used ethnic categories; eleven officials remained. Ponnambalam Ramanathan's selection mattered, but this was a long way from one adult, one vote.

The Ceylon National Congress began in 1919 with Ponnambalam Arunachalam as president and aimed at a common reform movement. Disagreement over a Colombo seat, withdrawal of Tamil leaders and later departures weakened it. Independence organizing crossed communities, but unity was argued over and could fracture.

Workers organized on their own terrain. The Ceylon Labour Union formed in 1922 and helped lead a general strike in 1923. Its suffrage demand explicitly crossed gender, race, religion and caste. The record also recalls resistance to a contribution that could require adult men to spend six days working on roads.

Universal adult suffrage arrived with the Donoughmore system in 1931, along with territorial representation and a State Council. Women did not receive the vote as a gift dropped from a government desk: Agnes de Silva and other members of the Society for Women's Suffrage testified before the commission and helped make the case.

Plantation labour politics reached the highest colonial offices in the 1937 Bracegirdle case. Bracegirdle opposed twelve-hour days and described brutality toward workers, women and children; the governor ordered him deported, prompting a political battle and commission. One manager's protest does not substitute for workers' own voices, but it exposed conditions to official scrutiny.

Representation changed by stages: Legislative Council from 1833, State Council from 1931 and a Soulbury Westminster model from 1944. Those forms should not be collapsed into full sovereignty. The first two operated under colonial rule, and even the 1944 redesign preceded legal independence.

The Ceylon Independence Act passed in 1947, and Ceylon became independent on 4 February 1948. The country later took the name Sri Lanka. The end of colonial Ceylon was a constitutional transition, not the disappearance of its peoples, languages, religions, labour struggles, family histories or memories of resistance.

ending.text: The map changes from ceylon-1815 to sri-lanka in 1945, but British colonial rule continued until 4 February 1948. Independent Ceylon inherited institutions, debts, inequalities, infrastructure and debates shaped during the colonial period; it later became the republic named Sri Lanka. Sinhala, Tamil and other communities did not begin in 1815 or end in 1945 or 1948. This card ends a colonial state period, not a people.
